classes.name: Banner Spear
classes.mechanic: Uses allies to create formation attacks.
classes.overview: Keep a dependable ally near your intended attack position. Explain the formation you need before a teammate commits to movement, then preserve an escape hex after attacking. A flexible movement card is often worth more than a stronger attack that cannot be positioned.

build.title: Formation captain
build.summary: Choose movement and formation flexibility first; add healing or banners only when the party can afford the setup. Plan attacks around allies' likely final positions, rather than asking everybody to rebuild their turn around yours.
steps: Identify the ally who can stay near the next formation target.
Move into a position that completes the required pattern without blocking the passage.
Use the formation, then preserve an alternative attack or movement for the next round.
build.cardSelection: Split your hand between formations you can satisfy with one dependable ally, a movement/reposition package and a small support package. Hail of Spears is a digitally confirmed multi-target option; the patch notes explicitly connect its target count to adjacent banner summons. Plan whether you can keep those banners in the relevant space before building around it. Bolstering Shout and Set for Charge are confirmed digital cards worth inspecting for the movement-and-attack sequence, rather than choosing every high-damage formation.
build.equipment: Prioritize reaching the correct formation hex over a generic damage boost. Defensive gear is useful if you are the hero who must hold that hex. Confirm that any attack item supports multi-target attacks before purchasing it for Hail of Spears.
build.perks: For an exploration-focused hand, inspect Into the Breach and consider whether the party wants you opening doors. For a static formation hand, favor accuracy and repeatable contribution over a perk tied to a job another hero performs.
build.pitfalls: A banner is an ally for some interactions but also occupies a tactically important position. A plan that needs several adjacent banners can congest the doorway and leave the spear or a teammate unable to attack.

classes.name: Blinkblade
classes.mechanic: Alternates slow preparation and fast expenditure using time tokens.
classes.overview: Treat a quiet round as preparation for the next engagement. Enter danger late when enemies have already acted, then use a fast turn to attack and leave. The strongest sequence is one you can afford twice, rather than a spectacular opener with no safe follow-up.

build.title: Tempo skirmisher
build.summary: Favor a useful slow action alongside each fast attack plan. Select mobility that ends in cover, and use fast rounds when an early kill prevents an enemy turn. Reserve an exit route before committing to several attacks.
steps: Choose a slow round where preparation will not leave an ally unsupported.
Spend the resulting tempo on a fast turn that removes a threat before it acts.
Move out of the remaining threat zone and check the next slow turn before ending.
build.cardSelection: Bring a fast payoff, a useful slow action and a retreat route in each rest cycle. Inspect Double Time when pursuing repeated fast effects: official digital notes confirm that it doubles fast effects in fast state. Reverse the Flow is a confirmed teleport-related option, but a destination occupied by another figure is illegal. Keep a cheaper sequence for rounds where you cannot afford the desired fast chain.
build.equipment: Initiative adjustment is valuable when it changes whether you kill or escape before an enemy acts. Movement equipment should support the exit as well as the approach. For a repeated-attack turn, verify whether an offensive item affects one attack, an action or a whole turn.
build.perks: Assess time-token economy before pure modifier damage. A perk that reduces a wasted slow round can improve several later turns. Revitalize and Headstart appear in digital notes, but their complete current text should be read before committing the build around either.
build.pitfalls: Do not copy a tabletop card screenshot without checking the selected card-layout option. The digital update adds an original-board-game layout setting, so confirm which fast and slow effect you are actually activating.

classes.name: Boneshaper
classes.mechanic: Maintains undead summons and pays attention to health as a summoning resource.
classes.overview: Summon where the next enemy engagement will happen. Keep lanes open so allies can move and the summons can reach their targets. Your own health is part of the engine, so a turn spent stabilizing yourself can protect several future summon turns.

build.title: Sustainable summon line
build.summary: Prefer repeatable summons, ways to direct or support them, and enough self-sustain to keep the engine operating. Build a useful front line without filling every doorway. Inspect summon focus before spending your command action.
steps: Place the first summon where it can reach the approaching enemy.
Keep the summoner safe while supporting the units already contributing.
Replace a fallen unit only when the replacement will have useful turns before the room ends.
build.cardSelection: Use a summon package with enough replacements to recover from a bad focus pattern, then reserve support and self-preservation. Bone Dagger is digitally confirmed to summon a skeleton. Flesh Shield is documented in a summon-damage prevention interaction, so inspect it when protecting a valuable unit. Putrid Cloud is not a poison source: recent official notes explicitly remove that incorrect behavior. Choose it for its actual current effect, not a remembered exploit.
build.equipment: Choose survival equipment based on the summoner's own incoming attacks and the health spent maintaining the engine. Do not assume an item that enhances your attack also enhances summon attacks. Recovery and movement can be more helpful than increasing the first skeleton's damage.
build.perks: Inspect Animate: digital notes confirm its healing applies to the Boneshaper even when a summon draws the modifier. A swarm making many attacks can value reliable self-sustain differently from a single durable summon. Compare that engine value with ordinary deck cleanup.
build.pitfalls: Putting every unit through a narrow entrance can leave most of your damage idle. Another trap is relying on old Putrid Cloud poison behavior, which the current patch history says was incorrect.

classes.name: Deathwalker
classes.mechanic: Creates and uses shadows to project attacks and reposition.
classes.overview: Establish your shadow supply before the party runs far ahead. Move the network toward the next fight while keeping your character outside unnecessary threat. Distinguish actions that create shadows from those that merely consume or reposition them.

build.title: Ranged shadow network
build.summary: Favor shadow generation, movement of shadows and repeatable ranged attacks from useful positions. Keep personal repositioning available so the character can catch up when the encounter moves. Spend shadows when the resulting removal prevents meaningful danger.
steps: Establish a way to generate shadows before loading the hand with consumers.
Advance the shadow positions toward the party's next target.
Attack through the network and reposition the character before it falls too far behind.
build.cardSelection: Separate the hand into shadow supply, shadow positioning and payoff. Call to the Abyss, Medium, Black Barrage and Strength of the Abyss are all present in digital notes. Black Barrage's Dark enhancement and Strength of the Abyss interaction are explicitly documented, making them candidates to inspect for a ranged damage sequence. Keep a generator when replacing a low-level attack; an additional consumer is not a substitute.
build.equipment: Buy movement or repositioning help if the character repeatedly trails the shadow network. Accuracy or attack enhancement is useful only if it applies to the actual attack being made. Avoid treating shadow tokens as independent units that automatically inherit the character's equipment.
build.perks: Favor modifier improvements that support your normal attack sequence before situational movement perks. Compare any shadow-related perk against the rate you generate and spend shadows, rather than selecting it because its name matches the theme.
build.pitfalls: Do not spend the same shadow twice in a sequence. Official digital fixes specifically restrict Strength of the Abyss interactions with attacks performed from multiple shadows; inspect the legal selection instead of assuming every displayed shadow is expendable.

classes.name: Drifter
classes.mechanic: Uses persistent tracks whose charges need maintenance.
classes.overview: Choose a clear job for the scenario instead of activating every persistent bonus. A straightforward melee plan gives the party a reliable point of contact, but movement and healing can matter more when objectives demand travel. Check your active tracks before selecting cards.

build.title: Reliable melee anchor
build.summary: Select a primary attack engine and a small supporting package of movement, sustain and track management. Upgrade consistency before adding a second unrelated damage plan. Evaluate equipment by how often it solves a problem during your normal turn.
steps: Choose the persistent track most relevant to the scenario's main job.
Use repeatable actions while watching how many charges remain.
Maintain the useful track before it disappears and leave another movement option available.
build.cardSelection: Choose one primary role and protect its charged persistent effects. A melee anchor needs repeatable attacks and enough movement to reach the next engagement; a support version needs healing and charge maintenance rather than the same damage hand with one heal added. Fortitude, Like the Wind and Against All Odds are digital-confirmed candidates. Check both halves when choosing which card to lose, since a future charge-management turn can matter more than an immediate attack.
build.equipment: A front-line build should solve repeated incoming attacks and movement first. A ranged or healing build can instead value reach and recovery. An item is not efficient merely because Drifter can technically use it in another role: match purchases to the persistent package actually active.
build.perks: Inspect whether a perk improves the normal role or tempts you to add another engine. Digital notes say Scavenger was redesigned, so read the current wording instead of importing a tabletop recommendation. Remove inconsistency when it repeatedly weakens the hero's routine contribution.
build.pitfalls: A route through allies can affect Like the Wind's token accounting in digital. Preview the actual movement and track change; do not calculate your remaining charges from the straight-line distance alone.

classes.name: Geminate
classes.mechanic: Switches between distinct melee and ranged forms.
classes.overview: Plan the current turn and the form you will need on the following turn. Count usable cards in each form before resting. The goal is to leave a coherent sequence available, with movement that makes the next form's attacks practical.

build.title: Balanced form cycle
build.summary: Keep a functional blend of attacks, movement and form-changing options across both forms. Spend a loss when it advances the objective or resolves a dangerous engagement, then rebalance future choices around the reduced hand.
steps: Count the currently usable cards in both forms.
Choose the next form based on reachable targets and remaining movement.
Execute a form transition that leaves a complete pair available for the following round.
build.cardSelection: Keep both forms equipped for the next cycle: a legal attack at the required distance, movement to reach that distance and a way to leave the form when needed. Hornbeetle Carapace, Reshape the Guise, Dragonfly Surge and Scarab Flight are digital-confirmed cards. Treat their element and defensive effects as specialized tools, and do not replace every flexible card with a conditional attack from your preferred form.
build.equipment: Movement tools are especially useful when they preserve a precise range band or the next form's access. Do not assume an item that adds ordinary range changes a printed precise-range restriction. Check each digital preview before spending resources on that combination.
build.perks: Acquired Resistance is mentioned in recent digital notes, which explicitly say it cannot prevent quest and event effects. Evaluate it for the effects it actually covers. An ordinary damage improvement may be preferable when you are already managing two forms and do not want another conditional trigger.
build.pitfalls: A defense card used only for movement can be productive; an element-consuming action canceled without performing its ability is not free engine progress. Check that the intended action resolves before counting its form or element consequences.

classes.name: Crashing Tide
classes.mechanic: Builds a persistent tide engine and uses water-related effects.
classes.overview: Look for a sustainable engagement where your setup can pay off over several rounds. Coordinate the front line so you are not repeatedly forced to abandon the space your engine supports. Treat water placement as a team movement decision.

build.title: Sustained tide bruiser
build.summary: Choose a focused set of tides that strengthens your most common actions. Add reliable movement before selecting another setup card. When possible, establish the engine near the fight rather than several turns behind it.
steps: Select a limited tide package that rewards the actions you expect to repeat.
Build the engine close enough to contribute to the current fight.
Keep water and movement choices compatible with allies crossing the same area.
build.cardSelection: Choose a limited set of tides that benefits the actions you repeat most often. Add movement and water manipulation rather than stacking every persistent effect. Rising Flood is digital-confirmed to relocate water, while Low Tide and Endless Cycle appear in tide-related fixes. Inspect these as an engine-and-recovery package; Drown beneath the Waves is a separately confirmed candidate whose elemental option must fit your supply.
build.equipment: Equip for the number of attacks you expect to receive while the tide engine is active. Movement equipment can keep an established engine relevant between rooms. Check whether water created by your character interacts with the current scenario's special rules instead of assuming every water tile behaves identically.
build.perks: Waterjet and Resilient Shell are named in digital patch notes. Compare their current effects against the actual frequency of your attacks and incoming damage. Choose a compact defensive or modifier improvement that supports the selected tide package rather than upgrading every possible role.
build.pitfalls: Water created by Coral can receive scenario-specific treatment. Official notes correct such an interaction in Rising Brine. Read the current special rules before using self-created water as though it were a universal protection against scenario damage.

classes.name: Deepwraith
classes.mechanic: Focuses on attack sequences, positioning and trophies.
classes.overview: Pick a priority enemy and count the movement needed to reach it and survive afterward. Coordinate concentrated attacks so you do not overkill a target a teammate would already remove. Use control and concealment as preparation for another productive turn.

build.title: Priority-target hunter
build.summary: Build around reliable access to a vulnerable target and several compatible attacks. Value initiative flexibility and escape movement. Avoid filling the hand with conditional burst that works only when the enemy and allies stand in exact positions.
steps: Choose a target whose removal matters before other allied attacks resolve.
Approach with a plan for the survivor and any enemies behind it.
Use the attack sequence, then protect the next turn with positioning rather than remaining exposed.
build.cardSelection: Separate trophy acquisition from trophy spending. Grim Trophies is digitally documented to grant its trophy on looting a loot bag, and its other effect requires enough trophies; budget around that requirement. Death Spiral and Staring into the Abyss are confirmed digital candidates to inspect for payoff. Preserve a repeatable attack and access to a second target when the planned victim dies early.
build.equipment: Prioritize tools that let you reach the intended victim and survive the following enemy actions. An accuracy or damage item should support a sequence that actually lands before the target dies to an ally. Check any Bane interaction against current card text and boss immunity.
build.perks: A trophy build needs a reliable acquisition rate before a perk that only improves spending. An aggressive multiple-attack hand may gain more from modifier consistency than from another conditional resource sink. Keep perks tied to your chosen target and rest-cycle plan.
build.pitfalls: Do not treat every loot-like object as a loot bag that fuels Grim Trophies. Do not spend the last trophies on a minor target if the next turn depends on a stronger effect. Digital notes also correct interactions between invisibility-like effects, movement and trophy abilities.

classes.name: Frozen Fist
classes.mechanic: Combines melee pressure, ice interaction and health-sensitive card recovery.
classes.overview: Health is a tactical budget rather than an invitation to absorb every attack. Spend it where recovery or offense creates a clear advantage, and agree with the party when healing is needed. Keep a route to the next objective after a melee exchange.

build.title: Controlled recovery brawler
build.summary: Take dependable attacks, practical movement and sustain before investing in elaborate element-dependent chains. Make a recovery plan at the same time as the attack plan. Keep track of the next round's health exposure, not just the current hit.
steps: Check the health cost of the intended attack and recovery sequence.
Engage where support is available and avoid adding unnecessary enemy attacks.
Recover only when the resulting hand and health state produce a safe following round.
build.cardSelection: Build around a repeatable attack-and-recovery rhythm, with movement that still works when no ideal element is available. One with the Mountain is digital-confirmed as a persistent effect with regeneration-related fixes. Plan the recovered card and health state together.

guides.title: Getting started: your first expedition
guides.summary: Begin with the tutorial and a party whose turns you understand. Win by following the scenario objective, preserving useful cards and preventing avoidable attacks.

sections.heading: What should you do before the first mission?
sections.body: Use the tutorial to learn what the interface asks you to confirm, then inspect each hero's available actions. Choose a small set of repeatable combinations rather than trying to memorize an entire class. The official new-player material recommends Story difficulty for beginners; lowering difficulty is a sensible learning tool when several systems are new at once. Keep the scenario objective visible. Clearing enemies, protecting a figure and reaching a location can demand very different decisions.

sections.heading: How should you plan each round?
sections.body: First identify the enemy or objective that can make the next round worse. Next check whether your hero can reach a legal position to contribute. Select actions with a fallback if that enemy dies before your turn. After enemy actions reveal, inspect movement and attack ranges before confirming your own movement. Spend a strong effect when it prevents a dangerous turn or completes an objective; preserve it when ordinary actions already solve the immediate problem.

sections.heading: What should you change after a defeat?
sections.body: Review the first round where the plan became expensive. Did the party open a room before everybody could act, spend losses without removing danger, or chase loot while an objective deteriorated? Fix that specific decision before changing the whole party. A retry is more useful when you bring a different opening sequence and a reason for it. Keep a brief note of the cards or movement tools you repeatedly wished you had.

guides.title: Choose a starting party that works together
guides.summary: Build a team around reliable contribution, movement and compatible positioning. Familiarity matters more than assigning every hero a traditional RPG role.

sections.heading: Which roles does a party need?
sections.body: Look for a way to remove dangerous enemies, a way to handle objectives and a way to survive rounds where removal is impossible. These jobs can overlap within one hero. A healer is not a substitute for preventing damage, and a durable hero cannot guarantee that every enemy will attack them. Think about where each character wants to stand, how long their engine needs to develop and whether they depend on the same element.

sections.heading: How do you check compatibility?
sections.body: Sketch the first two rounds for each candidate pair. Ask whether both heroes can reach useful positions without occupying the same narrow passage. A formation user needs dependable allied positioning; a summoner needs routes through the front line; an element user needs supply. Choose at least one hero whose normal turn remains useful when the other is setting up. At higher player counts, discuss doorway traffic before adding another melee or summon-heavy plan.

sections.heading: What causes a seemingly strong team to struggle?
sections.body: Several individually powerful classes can all want a setup round, the same element or the same attack hex. Their theoretical damage then arrives too late. Diagnose the repeated conflict rather than assuming the classes are weak. Change a few card choices, agree who enters a room first and keep one flexible responder. Test the revised routine on an ordinary encounter before making major campaign commitments or purchasing equipment intended for a complicated combination.

guides.title: Plan two-card turns with useful fallbacks
guides.summary: A good pair covers the intended action and an alternative. Think about your final position and the next round before committing to maximum damage.

sections.heading: How do you build a reliable turn?
sections.body: Start with a concrete outcome: remove an enemy, cross a room, protect an ally or interact with an objective. Then identify the movement and action needed to accomplish it. Check that the two chosen cards actually supply those jobs together. For the tabletop rules underlying the adaptation, turns generally combine a top action from one card with a bottom action from the other; follow the digital interface and any current special rules when resolving exceptions.

sections.heading: What makes a fallback useful?
sections.body: Imagine that your intended target is defeated before you act. Can the same pair reach another enemy, collect useful loot safely or move toward the next objective? A fallback need not be equally powerful; it should keep the round productive. Pick initiative with the action in mind. Acting early is helpful when prevention matters, while acting later can let enemies approach. Check whether the square you want will still be reachable after allied movement.

sections.heading: How should you react after the reveal?
sections.body: Read enemy actions before moving. If their attack or range changes, reconsider where your character should finish. Avoid confirming the planned movement automatically simply because it was correct during selection. Sometimes the strongest revision is to do less damage and end safely. After the round, look at what remains in hand so that this pair does not leave every useful movement option in discard when the objective shifts.

guides.title: Use initiative to manage exposure
guides.summary: Initiative is a positioning resource. Choose when a hero becomes exposed, and plan the next round before stepping into melee.

sections.heading: When is acting early useful?
sections.body: Early action is valuable when you can remove or disable a dangerous enemy before it acts, move away from a threatened position or secure an objective in time. It does not automatically make a turn safe. Moving toward several enemies early can simply give all of them convenient attacks. Compare the effect you will achieve with the attacks that your final position permits.

sections.heading: When can acting late help?
sections.body: A later turn can let approaching enemies spend movement without reaching you. You may then move in and attack after their turns. This is a planning technique rather than a guaranteed rule: ranged attacks, unusually large movement and special scenario behavior can defeat the expectation. Check the revealed enemy actions and keep another option. If you end next to a survivor, plan whether the following hand can act early enough to leave or finish the fight.

sections.heading: What are the common failures?
sections.body: Players sometimes choose a late turn because they remember an enemy was slow last round. Its next action can be different. Others use a late approach but forget that their remaining cards cannot provide a quick following turn. Treat initiative as a sequence across rounds, not a single number. Discuss who needs the first attack and who is waiting for a doorway to clear. Avoid sharing exact hidden information when your chosen ruleset restricts it.

guides.title: Resting, loss cards and exhaustion
guides.summary: Cards are a scenario budget. Rest when it supports a useful sequence, and spend losses when their effect justifies reducing later options.

sections.heading: Why does card conservation matter?
sections.body: The number of turns you can continue acting depends on your available cards, not only your current health. A loss action can be excellent, but spending one early reduces what you can recover on later cycles. Evaluate the entire encounter: a burst that removes an enemy before several attacks can save resources, while a flashy attack into a nearly defeated target may buy nothing.

sections.heading: How should you prepare for a rest?
sections.body: Inspect which cards are in hand, discard, active and lost before the next round. Identify the engine piece you cannot afford to lose and check how your chosen rest works in the digital interface. If the room is under control, coordinate a safe rest window rather than leaving one hero alone to absorb the next wave. A long rest may help recover appropriate spent equipment, but it also changes that round's contribution.

sections.heading: How do you avoid running out near the objective?
sections.body: Do not automatically spend a loss on every opening hand. Estimate how much travelling and fighting remains, and keep movement available for the final stretch. When the party repeatedly exhausts shortly before victory, compare unnecessary setup cards and avoidable defensive losses before reducing damage output indiscriminately. If a scenario has a clock, excessive conservation is also a mistake: use powerful effects to shorten the dangerous section. Check class-specific recovery and scenario exceptions rather than applying one universal stamina formula.

guides.title: Open doors with the whole party ready
guides.summary: A doorway is a change in information and exposure. Enter new rooms when the team can respond, with movement and fallback actions available.

sections.heading: What should happen before opening a room?
sections.body: Read the current objective and consider whether opening the next area is necessary now. Check the party's position, hand readiness and unresolved threats. An isolated hero at the door may reveal enemies while the rest of the team is resting or several turns away. Where possible, finish urgent work in the current room and approach as a coordinated group.

sections.heading: How do you handle the reveal?
sections.body: Leave enough of the opener's turn to respond after the room appears. Inspect enemies, objectives, terrain and the special-rules panel rather than treating the new space as a standard kill room. Choose an initial fighting line that leaves allies room to enter. Decide whether to advance, withdraw toward the doorway or use ranged pressure. The correct choice depends on the revealed actions and objective, not the number of enemies alone.

sections.heading: What goes wrong most often?
sections.body: A common failure is ending movement directly inside the doorway, making the opener a convenient target and obstructing friendly access. Another is sending summons toward the next room without a character ready to manage the door and subsequent positioning. Avoid using every flexible resource immediately before a reveal. If an objective requires speed, prepare the fast entry before opening rather than discovering afterward that every movement card is unavailable. After a difficult attempt, record which opening position gave the enemies the most free value.

guides.title: Read enemy actions before choosing your route
guides.summary: Enemy behavior is a source of planning information. Inspect the revealed action and reachable attack positions instead of reacting only to distance.

sections.heading: What should you inspect?
sections.body: For each dangerous enemy group, read the current action, initiative and relevant status effects. Determine which attacks can actually reach a party member and whether movement is present on that action. Do not assume every enemy moves and attacks on every turn. In the digital version, use available previews and tooltips, but check the action text when an apparent route seems surprising.

sections.heading: How do you make a safer movement decision?
sections.body: Compare two or three possible ending hexes. Ask which enemy attacks each one permits, whether an ally blocks your escape and whether the next objective remains reachable. When possible, remove an enemy that has a threatening action before spending damage on one that cannot contribute this round. Reconsider the threat after each kill or forced movement, since paths and focus opportunities may change.

sections.heading: Which assumptions should you avoid?
sections.body: Do not expect a monster to take a damaging route if it has a safe way to perform its attack. Do not rely on a remembered tabletop tiebreak when the digital implementation or scenario rule shows something different. Exact focus resolution is a rules question; this guide recommends checking it rather than inventing a shortcut. When a preview appears inconsistent, read the special rules and active effects, then document the situation with the enemy action and board position before reporting a bug.

guides.title: Plan element generation and consumption
guides.summary: Elements are shared timing resources. Name the intended consumer before building a turn around an infusion or empowered action.

sections.heading: What should you establish first?
sections.body: Identify which actions in the party create elements and which ones need them. An element-dependent attack should have a realistic source, rather than assuming the board will provide it. Use the digital element display and current card wording to check availability and timing. Tabletop timing is useful context, but do not infer that an element created during an action is immediately usable by another part of that same turn.

sections.heading: How do you coordinate supply?
sections.body: Plan the generator and intended consumer as a sequence. Check initiative, remaining enemies and whether somebody else could need the same resource. Give the consumer a useful unempowered option in case the original sequence becomes impossible. A modest reliable action can outperform a powerful card that repeatedly misses its element. If the party has two hungry engines, deliberately divide responsibilities or bring additional generation rather than discovering the conflict mid-round.

sections.heading: When should you abandon the planned combination?
sections.body: If the target dies, a teammate must rest or a scenario effect changes the board, evaluate the new situation instead of spending an element merely because it was prepared. Preserve it for a more useful legal action when possible. Avoid taking an entire setup turn for a benefit that no longer advances the objective. After the mission, note which element was consistently missing and change that part of the hand before adding more conditional consumers.

guides.title: Use conditions to prevent expensive turns
guides.summary: Conditions matter most when they change the enemy's next useful action. Check timing and immunity, and compare prevention with immediate removal.

sections.heading: How do you choose a condition target?
sections.body: Read the enemy's revealed action first. A movement-related condition matters differently for a distant melee enemy than for one already in attack range. An attack-preventing effect is most valuable on a dangerous attacker that would otherwise survive. Conditions should solve the threat in front of you rather than decorate an enemy that the party is already certain to defeat.

sections.heading: How should you handle conditions on allies?
sections.body: Inspect what the condition prevents and when it ends. Decide whether to remove it, play a useful unaffected action or reposition to make the next round safer. Check the digital tooltip rather than relying on a remembered Gloomhaven interaction. Some heroes deliberately interact with negative conditions, but that does not mean every condition or every timing window helps them. Coordinate before applying a cost or accepting transferred harm.

sections.heading: What are the frequent mistakes?
sections.body: Do not assume that a boss accepts every condition; inspect its immunities and scenario rules. Do not build a turn around a status effect that expires before the intended follow-up. Healing, condition removal and attack prevention can have different outcomes, so read the ability rather than treating them as interchangeable. When a combination seems exceptionally strong, verify each step separately: legal target, application, duration and the effect on the actual enemy action. Revise the plan if any step fails.

guides.title: Keep summons productive without blocking allies
guides.summary: Summons need useful paths and targets. Plan their next activation, not just the hex where they appear.

sections.heading: Where should a summon enter play?
sections.body: Look at the next fight and the friendly movement lanes before choosing a placement. A unit summoned far behind the party may spend several turns travelling; one placed too far forward may immediately take unnecessary attacks. Choose a position that lets it contribute soon without closing the only passage. Consider whether your hero has time to support the summon before enemies act.

sections.heading: What should you inspect on later turns?
sections.body: Check the summon's likely focus, movement and available attack position before spending a command or support action. Make sure the target remains reachable after allied movement. Your character's best action may be clearing an obstacle in the team's plan, such as removing a blocking enemy, rather than adding another summon. When a fight ends, decide how the existing units will reach the next useful engagement.

sections.heading: How do you avoid common losses?
sections.body: A summon is not automatically an expendable shield, especially if replacing it costs important cards or health. Compare the prevented damage with the future contribution you lose. Be especially careful around retaliation, area attacks and scenarios that damage particular tiles. Tabletop guidance does not prove every digital command interaction, so follow current card text and the interface. If a summon stops unexpectedly, inspect legal paths and focus before assuming the game failed. Record the situation if the preview and resolved behavior disagree.

guides.title: Choose equipment for your actual turn sequence
guides.summary: Buy or craft tools that solve repeated problems. Check the digital item's timing, recovery and requirements before investing resources.

sections.heading: How do you identify a useful purchase?
sections.body: Review the last mission and choose a concrete problem: missing a destination by one step, taking an avoidable attack or failing to land a critical hit. An item that reliably fixes that problem is easier to value than a damage bonus with an elaborate condition. Consider how frequently the tool will be available and whether using it competes with another equipment slot.

sections.heading: How do you fit it into a build?
sections.body: Write out one normal turn using the item, including its timing and the action it modifies. Check whether it affects the character's own action, an ally's granted action or a summon; these are not necessarily equivalent. Read whether the item becomes spent or lost and how it can return. Test the combination in the digital interface before treating it as the foundation of a permanent build.

sections.heading: What should you verify before crafting?
sections.body: Use the current digital Codex or crafting screen for the recipe, availability and upgrade prerequisites. Do not import a tabletop item number or a community nickname as proof of digital parity. Keep enough resources for an agreed outpost priority if the party depends on it. A rarely used item can still be a good answer to a specific scenario, but distinguish specialist equipment from everyday gear. After several missions, replace assumptions with observed use: how often did it activate, and did it change the outcome?

guides.title: Plan outpost upgrades around the next bottleneck
guides.summary: Choose upgrades for the capabilities they unlock and the resources the party needs. Read the current digital phase flow before leaving town.

sections.heading: What should you review on returning?
sections.body: Inspect the current outpost state, available construction and the next campaign objective. Separate immediate repairs or mandatory choices from optional improvements. The digital adaptation changes aspects of the outpost flow, and 1.0 includes further interface and building changes, so use the current screen order instead of copying a tabletop checklist verbatim. Review the consequences before advancing past a confirmation.

sections.heading: How do you choose between upgrades?
sections.body: Name the problem the party wants to solve: limited crafting choices, equipment access, a campaign requirement or settlement resilience. Compare upgrades by the capability they enable rather than by their visual prominence. Check the actual resource cost and prerequisites on screen. Coordinate spending before individual characters craft specialist equipment, especially when both choices rely on the same scarce materials.

sections.heading: How do you prevent waste?
sections.body: Avoid a rigid universal build order. The useful choice depends on what your campaign has unlocked and which resources have accumulated. Keep a short list of the next two desired improvements, then revisit it after discoveries and events. When a new building introduces a subsystem, inspect it before committing the rest of the budget elsewhere. Exact upgrade costs, defense values and unlock conditions require current digital verification; this guide deliberately does not replace the building screen with unverified numbers. Recheck the choice whenever a new campaign unlock changes the available options.

guides.title: Collect resources without sacrificing the mission
guides.summary: Loot has campaign value, but an unnecessary detour can cost more than it earns. Gather along useful routes and coordinate crafting needs.

sections.heading: When is collecting loot worthwhile?
sections.body: Compare the movement and action cost with the current objective and threats. A token on the route to a productive attack can be nearly free; one behind the party can require an entire round and leave the collector exposed. Check whether the scenario is time-sensitive before planning a collection turn. Completing the objective should remain the reason the party is in the room.

sections.heading: How do you make looting safer?
sections.body: Decide who can collect without losing their main contribution. Keep useful movement available after the pickup and avoid creating a target for several enemy attacks. If a fight is nearly controlled, coordinate the final actions so one hero does not end the encounter before a planned legal pickup. Follow the actual objective completion behavior rather than assuming you can always explore afterward.

sections.heading: How should campaign needs influence the choice?
sections.body: Before departing, identify whether the party is saving for a particular building or useful crafted tool. That gives resource collection a purpose without dictating every combat turn. After returning, check the recipe and construction requirements in the digital interface before spending. Do not assume resources can always be freely exchanged between every inventory or campaign pool. If collection repeatedly causes failed missions, shorten the detour budget and prioritize tokens reached by actions that also advance the scenario.

guides.title: Coordinate co-op turns without slowing every round
guides.summary: Agree on outcomes, movement lanes and shared resources. Use short planning calls so everybody can contribute while retaining flexibility.

sections.heading: What should the party discuss?
sections.body: Name the dangerous enemy, the objective to advance and the positions that must stay clear. Tell teammates if your turn depends on an ally being nearby, an element being available or a target surviving. Discuss a contingency for the hero most likely to open a room or become exposed. Follow your selected ruleset's restrictions on sharing hidden card information.

sections.heading: How do you avoid planning gridlock?
sections.body: Assign outcomes rather than scripting every click. One hero can handle an exposed attacker while another prepares the doorway, with a third keeping a support option available. After enemy actions reveal, update only the decisions that changed. Let the active player finish confirmations clearly before another player triggers an interaction that depends on them. If somebody must step away, agree how the party will pause or reconnect rather than assuming every action can be undone safely.

sections.heading: What should you do when a session misbehaves?
sections.body: The 1.0 notes include networking improvements, but no release can promise every session is faultless. Record the scenario, turn order and action that preceded an unexpected result. Check whether the problem is an objective rule or a card interaction before calling it desynchronization. Avoid repeatedly advancing the session while clients display different states. Use the game's supported recovery flow, and include concise reproduction information in any report. After the session, adjust one recurring coordination problem rather than blaming an entire class or player.

guides.title: Read scenario objectives before building a hand
guides.summary: The objective defines the best turn. Prepare movement, interaction and survival tools for the actual win condition rather than assuming every encounter is a full clear.

sections.heading: What belongs on your pre-mission checklist?
sections.body: Read the objective, special rules and visible terrain information before finalizing the hand. Identify whether the party needs to defeat enemies, protect an ally, move a figure, collect objects or interact with locations. Note any failure condition and whether the scenario changes normal behavior. In digital 1.0, the official notes specifically mention expanded scenario special-rule information; consult that panel when a situation looks unusual.

sections.heading: How do you adapt the build?
sections.body: Choose enough movement to reach the important spaces and enough repeatable contribution to handle threats on the way. A stationary engine that shines in a long fight may need fewer setup effects in a travelling scenario. Assign objective jobs to heroes who can perform them without abandoning the party's only reliable damage or support. Keep a substitute in case that hero becomes delayed, disabled or exhausted.

sections.heading: How do you learn from a failed attempt?
sections.body: Identify whether defeat came from combat pressure, wasted travel or misunderstanding the rule. Change the relevant part of the hand and opening route. Do not increase damage automatically if the real issue was reaching an interaction point. Check whether special objects obey ordinary targeting and movement rules before spending a powerful effect on them. Historical patch notes confirm that individual quests have had unique interactions; they are a reason to read current rules carefully, not a guarantee that an old workaround remains necessary.

news.summary: The full PC release is available, with the campaign finale and the final playable hero.
news.body: Frosthaven's full PC release arrived on October 15, 2026. The official launch announcement confirms a complete campaign and all seventeen playable heroes. The digital-exclusive Road to Frosthaven introduction provides an onboarding route, while the completed Codex collects information about the game's world. The update also adds opening and hero-unlock cinematics and further cooperative-play improvements. Existing Early Access owners receive the full release through an update, and the official FAQ says existing saves remain compatible. Players continuing an established campaign should read the new scenario special-rules panels and revisit the outpost interface, both of which are called out in the 1.0 notes. A patch announcement is a record of developer changes rather than a promise that every reported issue is resolved in every situation.
